name: poison-pill
intent: Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation.
problem: A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?
context: In-process or broker-mediated producer-consumer systems with a FIFO work queue, a fixed set of long-lived consumers (threads, coroutines, actors) that block when the queue is empty, and a shutdown requirement that work already accepted by the queue be drained before the consumers exit - typically deployment, signal handling or test teardown.
benefits: Graceful drain: work already accepted by the queue is completed before the consumers exit, so a shutdown cannot silently drop buffered items.
No new control channel: the shutdown signal rides the work queue itself, so consumers need no extra flag, latch or out-of-band protocol.
Cooperative and race-free to reason about: each consumer decides when to exit, and FIFO ordering makes "after the last item" well defined.
Reuses the runtime's blocking/suspending take, so the shutdown path costs no polling and no extra wake-up machinery.
Works on any channel with FIFO semantics, including bounded queues, where the same backpressure protects the drain.
Deterministic teardown for tests: an explicit stop item makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
tradeoffs: One pill per consumer: the injector must know how many consumers share the queue, and the count is easy to get wrong - a lost pill leaves a worker blocked forever, an extra pill stops another worker's backlog early.
The signal is in-band: the sentinel shares the data plane with real work, needs a reserved type/tag that cannot collide with payloads, and anyone who can enqueue can stop the consumers.

Ordering is load-bearing: a pill enqueued before pending work stops the consumer early, a duplicated pill causes premature exit, and the protocol is only safe on a FIFO channel whose producers have stopped first.
No completion feedback: the pill asks consumers to stop but does not report that they did; a join/acknowledgement step and a deadline remain the caller's responsibility.
Cooperative only: a consumer stuck in a long task or blocked downstream never dequeues the pill, so a hard-stop mechanism (interrupt, cancellation token, kill) is still required as a fallback.
Does not cross process or broker boundaries: consumers you do not control never see the sentinel, so remote or third-party consumers need the transport's own close/stop facility.

participants.responsibility: Enqueues work items and, after the last item, one pill per consumer; must stop enqueuing real work before the pills so that the drain is complete.
Loops on the queue with the runtime's blocking take; on dequeuing the pill it finishes the current item, releases resources and exits.
A reserved message, value or tag distinct from every work payload, meaning "no more work"; the only in-band signal the consumer must recognise.
FIFO transport that delivers the pill after all preceding work and blocks consumers while it is empty.
Knows the number of consumers, injects exactly that many pills once production has stopped, joins the consumers and escalates to hard cancellation if they miss the deadline.

use_cases: Signal-driven shutdown of an in-process worker pool: the SIGTERM handler stops accepting work, then enqueues one pill per worker so the backlog is processed before the process exits.
Batch importers and ETL stages whose consumers block on a work queue and must finish the current batch before a run is considered complete.
Test harnesses and simulations: an explicit stop message makes thread-based systems deterministic to shut down, without sleeps or guessed timeouts.
Actor systems: a reserved stop message (for example Akka PoisonPill) terminates an actor after the messages already queued for it have been handled.
Log and event writers where the last records must reach the sink before consumers release their buffers and files.
Bounded-queue stages in a pipeline: pills travel the same backpressured channel as work, so upstream cannot keep producing after the stop decision.
Kubernetes pod shutdown: containers receive SIGTERM, workers stop pulling from the job queue, drain in-flight tasks, then exit within the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window.
Redis/Bull queue workers: a shutdown signal pushes a sentinel via BLPOP so workers exit cleanly without losing the right to process pending tasks.
Akka Streams and similar streaming frameworks: the GraphStage signals completion via onPull/downstream cancellation, which is the materialised equivalent of a poison pill.

Redis Streams consumer groups: XREADGROUP with block timeout naturally returns when the stream is empty; a special ID (e.g. ">") polling loop plus a shared shutdown flag replaces the in-process sentinel.

Broker-level poison message isolation: in Kafka, RabbitMQ, or Azure Service Bus, a permanently failing message (deserialisation error, validation failure) blocks a partition/consumer indefinitely; DLQ-based routing (publish to dead-letter topic after N retries, then commit offset and continue) is the broker-level analogue that prevents one poison message from halting the entire pipeline.

Kubernetes preStop hooks + pill drain: a container's lifecycle preStop hook can enqueue a sentinel into an in-process work queue while the orchestrator grants terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain to complete, ensuring zero work-drop during rolling updates.

Azure Service Bus competing-consumers workers: when a worker receives a shutdown notification it completes its current PeekLock message, then calls Abandon on any held locks before unregistering; Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues handle the poison-message variant when a message exceeds MaxDeliveryCount and cannot be delivered.

Akka hierarchical actor trees: sending PoisonPill to a parent actor stops it after all queued messages ahead of the pill are processed, and automatically sends stop messages to all children in bottom-up order; this is the idiomatic way to orchestrate ordered multi-actor shutdown.

Non-blocking retry architectures (RabbitMQ): rather than local Thread.sleep retries that block the consumer thread, use server-side TTL queues with Dead Letter Exchange routing to implement exponential backoff, keeping the consumer responsive to new messages and to shutdown pills.

Java's JDK BlockingQueue worker pools: because BlockingQueue has no built-in close, producers can enqueue a unique end-of-stream object after all work; each consumer takes until that sentinel and then the coordinator joins workers.

Python multiprocessing worker pools: multiprocessing.Queue/JoinableQueue supports FIFO task delivery with sentinel values and join-based drain tracking; send one sentinel per worker and join them after the queue is exhausted.

Akka Classic actors: PoisonPill is enqueued in the mailbox and processed after already queued messages, while Akka Typed requires an explicit Stop/Shutdown protocol; choose the API that matches the actor model.
avoid_when: The executor or collection already has a completion protocol - ExecutorService.shutdown()/close(), BlockingCollection.CompleteAdding(), close(ch), Thread::Queue#close, AsyncStream.finish(); use that instead of adding an in-band sentinel.
Hard termination is required (a hung consumer, a deadline): the pill is cooperative and cannot interrupt work in progress; use a cancellation token or interrupt with a hard-kill fallback.
Consumers are remote or independently deployed, or a broker topic has consumer groups you do not own: a sentinel cannot address them - use the broker's consumer-stop/close API.
There is exactly one producer and one consumer, and the consumer is awaited as a future: completing the input or dropping the sender is simpler and cannot be miscounted.
Heterogeneous consumers share one queue and must stop at different times: counting pills per consumer type is brittle - a dedicated shutdown channel or flag is clearer.
The queue is unordered or priority-based: a pill's FIFO position is meaningless; the drain guarantee does not hold.
anti_patterns: Confusing the shutdown sentinel with a poison message: an undeliverable or malformed message belongs to Invalid Message Channel or Dead Letter Channel handling, not to consumer shutdown - the shared "poison" name causes real design mistakes.
Broadcasting a single pill to a multi-consumer queue: one consumer dequeues it and exits while the rest block forever; inject one pill per consumer or close the channel instead.
Enqueuing pills before the backlog (or letting producers keep adding afterwards), so consumers stop early and queued work is dropped without a trace.
Using a magic payload value (null, -1, empty string) as the sentinel on a queue that can legitimately carry it; the consumer stops on real data.
A pill protocol with no join: shutdown looks successful while workers are still running, or hangs because nothing waits for them.
Relying on a pill to abort a consumer stuck in a long task; it is never dequeued, and graceful shutdown turns into a hang.
Enqueuing a single pill for all consumers on a shared queue: the first consumer takes it and exits, leaving the rest blocked forever.

Confusing "poison pill message" (a permanently failing record that blocks a partition in Kafka/RabbitMQ and requires DLQ routing) with "poison pill sentinel" (the cooperative shutdown signal); these are two distinct patterns that share the word "poison".
design_principles: Explicit lifecycle: a consumer's stop condition is a first-class part of the protocol, not an ambient flag or a timeout.
Ordering determines semantics: "drain then stop" is only well defined on a FIFO channel, so the channel's ordering guarantee is part of the pattern.
Symmetry of creation and destruction: whoever starts the consumers owns the pills (one per consumer) and joins them.
Prefer the runtime's completion primitive over an in-band sentinel when one exists (channel close, CompleteAdding, Queue#close); the sentinel is for queues that lack one.
Separate draining from aborting: a cooperative stop finishes accepted work, while abrupt termination is a different mechanism with different guarantees.
Least knowledge: producers know only the sentinel contract, consumers only the queue; neither needs the other's identity.

Poison is not the same as "bad message": a poison pill is a normal sentinel for cooperative shutdown; a poison message is a malformed payload requiring Dead Letter Queue handling - conflating the two causes architectural mistakes.
best_practices: Inject exactly one pill per consumer, after the last work item, from a single close()/shutdown() helper so producers cannot forget, duplicate or reorder the pills.
Make the pill runtime-distinguishable - a dedicated type, tag field or enum - never a magic payload value, and document the sentinel contract next to the queue's declaration.
Keep the pill on the same FIFO channel as work; do not route it through a priority lane, or the drain guarantee breaks.
Join every consumer after the pills and enforce a bounded deadline; escalate to interrupt/cancel if a consumer misses it rather than reporting a clean shutdown.
Never send the sentinel across process or broker boundaries; use the transport's own consumer-stop facility there.
Test the shutdown path itself: assert that all queued work completed before exit and that a missing pill is detected (deadline) rather than hidden by daemon threads or process exit.
When the queue already offers a completion API (Close, Complete, CompleteAdding, close token), use it and keep the sentinel only for queues without one.
Combine the sentinel with a bounded deadline and a hard-cancel escalation: a missing pill should never result in a process that hangs indefinitely.
On ordered/brokered queues, consider a circuit breaker that prevents a single poison message from blocking the head of the queue; route it to a DLQ after N retries instead of retrying in place.
Distinguish poison-pill shutdown (cooperative drain) from Dead Letter Queue handling (malformed/unprocessable messages); these are two separate concerns sharing the word "poison".

In actor hierarchies (Akka, Erlang OTP), prefer the built-in stop/terminate signal (PoisonPill in Akka, link/exit in Erlang) over a manual queue-based pill; the runtime handles child ordering and resource cleanup.

In weakly-ordered memory models, ensure the pill is published with proper synchronisation after all preceding work items; on ARM/POWER architectures a plain write to a shared queue field may not be visible to the consumer before the pill is dequeued.
